cities.name: Petra
cities.description: Petra is a historic city in southern Jordan famous for its rock-cut architecture and water conduit system. Established as the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom around 312 BC, it was lost to the Western world until Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt rediscovered it in 1812. Known as the Rose City for the color of its sandstone cliffs, Petra was a major trading hub connecting Arabia, Egypt, and the Mediterranean.

cities.name: Pompeii
cities.description: Pompeii was a prosperous Roman city buried under volcanic ash and pumice following the catastrophic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. Rediscovered in 1748, excavations have revealed remarkably preserved streets, buildings, and even human remains. It offers one of the most complete snapshots of Roman daily life ever found.

cities.name: Machu Picchu
cities.description: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel situated on a mountain ridge above the Sacred Valley in Peru. Built at the height of the Inca Empire around 1450 AD, it was abandoned just over a century later during the Spanish conquest. Largely unknown to the outside world until American historian Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.

cities.name: Troy
cities.description: Troy is an ancient city on the northwestern coast of modern Turkey, immortalized in Homer's Iliad as the setting of the legendary Trojan War. Believed to be mythical for centuries, archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann began excavations in 1870 and discovered evidence of multiple ancient settlements stacked upon one another, confirming its historical existence.

cities.name: El Dorado
cities.description: El Dorado is a legendary city of gold sought by Spanish conquistadors throughout the 16th and 17th centuries. The myth originated from indigenous South American stories of a chieftain who covered himself in gold dust. Countless expeditions were launched into the Amazon basin and Andes mountains in search of this fabled city, all ending in failure.

cities.name: Atlantis
cities.description: Atlantis is a legendary island civilization first described by the ancient Greek philosopher Plato around 360 BC. According to Plato, it was a naval superpower that sank into the ocean in a single day and night. Whether purely allegorical or based on a real event, Atlantis remains one of history's most enduring mysteries and a subject of endless speculation.

cities.name: Carthage
cities.description: Carthage was a powerful ancient city-state founded by Phoenician settlers on the coast of North Africa around 814 BC. It became one of the greatest commercial and military powers of the ancient Mediterranean, rivaling Rome in its influence. The city was completely destroyed by Rome in 146 BC at the end of the Third Punic War.

cities.name: Angkor
cities.description: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire and once the largest pre-industrial city in the world, covering over 400 square kilometers. At its peak in the 12th century, it was home to nearly one million people. The temple complex of Angkor Wat remains the largest religious monument on earth. The city was gradually abandoned between the 14th and 15th centuries.

cities.name: Mohenjo-daro
cities.description: Mohenjo-daro was one of the largest settlements of the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation, built around 2500 BC. It was one of the world's earliest major urban settlements, featuring sophisticated city planning, a drainage system, and multi-story buildings. The city was abandoned around 1700 BC for reasons still debated by scholars.

cities.name: Tikal
cities.description: Tikal was one of the largest cities of the ancient Maya civilization, located in the rainforests of northern Guatemala. At its height between 200 and 900 AD, it was home to over 100,000 people. The city contains some of the most impressive Maya architecture ever discovered, including massive temple-pyramids rising above the jungle canopy.

cities.name: Babylon
cities.description: Babylon was one of the most important cities of the ancient world, serving as the capital of the Babylonian Empire in modern-day Iraq. Famous for the legendary Hanging Gardens — one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World — and the Tower of Babel, Babylon was a center of culture, science, and trade for centuries before its decline.

cities.name: Teotihuacan
cities.description: Teotihuacan was a massive pre-Columbian city located in the Basin of Mexico. At its height around 450 AD it was one of the largest cities in the world with a population of over 125,000. Despite extensive excavation, the identity of the civilization that built it remains unknown. The city was mysteriously abandoned around 550 AD.

cities.name: Skara Brae
cities.description: Skara Brae is a well-preserved Neolithic village located on the Bay of Skaill in Orkney, Scotland. Occupied from roughly 3180 BC to 2500 BC, it is older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramids. The village was buried under sand dunes for centuries until a severe storm in 1850 uncovered the ruins, revealing stone furniture and artifacts in remarkable condition.

cities.name: Cahokia
cities.description: Cahokia was the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, located near present-day St. Louis. At its peak around 1100 AD it had a population of 10,000 to 20,000 people — larger than contemporary London. The city is famous for its enormous earthen mounds, the largest of which is Monks Mound, a massive structure larger at its base than the Great Pyramid of Giza.

cities.name: Palenque
cities.description: Palenque was a Maya city-state in southern Mexico that reached its height between 500 and 700 AD under the rule of Pakal the Great. The city contains some of the finest Maya architecture, sculpture, and bas-relief carvings ever discovered. It was abandoned around 900 AD and swallowed by the jungle, remaining hidden until the 18th century.

cities.name: Akrotiri
cities.description: Akrotiri was a Minoan Bronze Age settlement on the island of Santorini in Greece, buried under volcanic ash following the massive Thera eruption around 1627 BC. The extraordinary preservation of buildings, frescoes, and artifacts has led many scholars to link Akrotiri to the legend of Atlantis. It was rediscovered during excavations in 1967.

cities.name: Great Zimbabwe
cities.description: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, a medieval Shona state in southern Africa. Built between the 11th and 15th centuries, its massive stone walls were constructed without mortar — a remarkable engineering achievement. The city was a major trade center connecting the African interior with coastal ports on the Indian Ocean.

cities.name: Chichen Itza
cities.description: Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people in the northern Maya lowlands of Mexico. A major focal point of the Maya world, the city underwent significant growth between 750 and 1200 AD. Its iconic pyramid El Castillo was engineered to create a serpent shadow effect during the spring and autumn equinoxes.

cities.name: Persepolis
cities.description: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, founded by Darius I around 518 BC. It served as the empire's grand showcase — a city built to impress visiting dignitaries with its monumental gateways, palace halls, and elaborate bas-reliefs. The city was destroyed by Alexander the Great in 330 BC in what is believed to have been an act of revenge.

cities.name: Leptis Magna
cities.description: Leptis Magna was one of the most spectacular cities of the Roman Empire, located on the Mediterranean coast of modern Libya. Founded by Phoenicians around 1100 BC, it flourished under Roman rule and became birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus. The city was gradually buried by sand dunes after the Arab conquest and remained preserved beneath them for centuries.

cities.name: Herculaneum
cities.description: Herculaneum was an ancient Roman town buried under volcanic ash and pyroclastic material during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD, alongside the more famous Pompeii. Unlike Pompeii, Herculaneum was buried under a deeper layer of material, preserving wooden furniture, food, and organic materials in extraordinary detail.

cities.name: Çatalhöyük
cities.description: Çatalhöyük is one of the world's oldest and best-preserved Neolithic settlements, located in south-central Turkey. Dating to around 7500 BC, it is considered one of humanity's first true towns, with a population estimated at between 3,000 and 8,000 people. Remarkably, its buildings had no ground-level doors — residents entered through roof hatches.
